title: Shifting to partnership: How the MoD wants industry to help deter and, if needed, fight
label: MoD · Defence industry relationship
summary: Ministers and senior Ministry of Defence officials told the Lords Industry and Regulators Committee how the Government intends to reshape procurement and industrial policy so industry can supply what the armed forces need faster and at scale. The witnesses said defence spending is rising, a delivery plan and an industry summit will clarify demand, procurement must become faster and more modular, and the MoD wants deeper partnerships with large firms and SMEs while guarding against fraud, supply‑chain fragility and hostile interference. They acknowledged practical challenges on testing, skills, regional spread and defining ‘buy British’, and promised further reporting.

glossary.definition: The Strategic Defence Review; set out how the UK should prepare and what the MoD must change.
Defence Investment Plan; a multi-year outline of what the MoD intends to spend and buy.
Defence Industrial Joint Council; a forum where government and industry coordinate strategy and delivery.
An MoD commercial unit used to speed emergency purchases, averaging about 50 days from idea to contract.
Large defence contractors who often sub-contract much of the work to smaller firms.
A capability to keep steady production of items (like munitions) in peacetime so output can surge in crisis.
Technology Readiness Level; a scale used to assess how mature a technology is.
A multinational defence programme mentioned as an example of allied procurement collaboration.

chapters.title: Context: why industry is part of deterrence
chapters.takeaway: Ministers say a stronger, more resilient defence industrial base is essential to deter and, if needed, fight — and defence spending is rising, giving clearer demand.

turns.speaker: The Chair
turns.text: We're focused on the new relationship the Strategic Defence Review proposed between Government and industry and how to give companies the confidence to respond to current threats.

turns.speaker: Wes Streeting
turns.text: My top priority is making sure we're ready to deter and, if needed, defeat those who would harm us. Industry is central: it supplies capabilities and the wider industrial surge capacity we'd need in a war.

turns.speaker: Wes Streeting
turns.text: Defence spending is rising: from 2.3% of GDP when we took office, set to be 2.7% next year, moving towards the NATO target of 3.5% by 2035 — that gives a clearer upward money trajectory.

turns.speaker: Wes Streeting
turns.text: There is some uncertainty about exact future envelopes, but the shortfall from earlier negotiations will be met at the Budget, and the Chancellor plans to set the pathway to 3.5% at the next spending review.

turns.speaker: The Chair
turns.text: When is the defence investment summit?

turns.speaker: Rupert Pearce
turns.text: The defence investment summit is on 1 December.

chapters.title: Procurement: speed, stratification and culture change
chapters.takeaway: The MoD accepts procurement has been slow and process-driven; it aims to stratify contracts, adopt faster models used for Ukraine, and change risk-averse culture.

turns.speaker: Lord Udny-Lister
turns.text: When will the defence and investment strategy be published, and will it give the signals industry needs to invest and tool up?

turns.speaker: Wes Streeting
turns.text: The defence industrial strategy and the investment plan already give a lot of direction and funding; the summit and conversion of the plan into a delivery plan will give more granular, investable signals.

turns.speaker: Rupert Pearce
turns.text: We're turning the high-level DIP into a delivery plan with industry, sharing detailed, granular work over the next six quarters so industry can plan and invest.

turns.speaker: Baroness Carberry of Muswell Hill
turns.text: Procurement can take six or seven years. Is the delivery plan addressing speed so capabilities arrive in time?

turns.speaker: Rupert Pearce
turns.text: Yes. We must stratify procurement: big platforms need different processes than routine systems. We should buy 'good enough' where appropriate, build modularly and develop in increments so we can move faster.

turns.speaker: Rupert Pearce
turns.text: Commercial X, used for Ukraine, has done over 1,000 procurements in three years with an average of 50 days from idea to contract. We want to scale, aim to reduce big-platform times from around six years to two, systems from three to one, and everything else to three months.

turns.speaker: Wes Streeting
turns.text: Since the SDR, major-platform times have already improved, so action is under way, not just words.

turns.speaker: Baroness Carberry of Muswell Hill
turns.text: Will you report back on how successful you are at speeding procurement?

turns.speaker: Rupert Pearce
turns.text: Yes. We have metrics tied to the SDR and the defence industrial strategy; we'll track and can bring that reporting back to the committee.

turns.speaker: Lord Camoys
turns.text: How do you change the MoD culture so it accepts greater risk and moves from process to outcomes?

turns.speaker: Wes Streeting
turns.text: Ministers must give political cover to tolerate reasonable risk. The armed forces and new ministerial leads back reform; we must be willing to accept some failures to iterate faster and encourage innovation.

turns.speaker: Rupert Pearce
turns.text: There is big internal risk aversion and a comfort in process. We must create new 'psychological safety' for faster decision-making. Ukraine work showed the department can operate at pace when it accepts more risk.

turns.speaker: Baroness Harding of Winscombe
turns.text: Do you need more top‑level political cover — from the Prime Minister or No.10 — to give officials the space to innovate?

turns.speaker: Wes Streeting
turns.text: The Prime Minister is engaged and a strong communicator; the Chancellor is closely involved. The DIP process has aligned Treasury and MoD on numbers, which helps create a higher‑trust environment to move faster.

chapters.title: SMEs, regional growth and skills
chapters.takeaway: The MoD wants many more SMEs to supply defence, with a single front door, standardised SME pathways, faster payments, funding and local skills plans — but delivery and scale are the challenge.

turns.speaker: Lord Best
turns.text: SMEs face big barriers: excessive paperwork, slow security clearances, late payments. Could we have a single front door, a standard SME contract and better payment terms?

turns.speaker: Wes Streeting
turns.text: The Defence Office for Small Business Growth, set up in January, is intended as the front door; it must scale. We need to improve payment practices and be a good partner on contract design and delivery.

turns.speaker: Rupert Pearce
turns.text: We already work with about 12,000 SMEs and do £5bn a year with them. The extra £2.5bn to 2028 is a 50% increase and will force behaviour change. The SME action plan covers capital access, payment terms and contracts.

turns.speaker: Ben White
turns.text: The Defence Office is the front door and we've launched accelerated commercial pathways for SMEs to use best practice and remove barriers. We also pay 94.6% of our contracts within five days and 99.9% within 30 days.

turns.speaker: Rupert Pearce
turns.text: On innovation, UK Defence Innovation spends about £400m a year on mid-stage technology. Competitions like Project Brakestop invited many SMEs and funded most to the next stage; that helps firms mature without 'betting the farm'.

turns.speaker: Lord Barber of Ainsdale
turns.text: As you move to deeper partnerships, how will you prevent cosy relationships, fraud or bid‑rigging?

turns.speaker: Wes Streeting
turns.text: We must balance partnership with robust competition and independent rules on social and economic value. The framework for 'buying British' will include checks to avoid undue discretion.

turns.speaker: Ben White
turns.text: The Treasury has set fraud targets and we are developing a department-wide fraud strategy; we're working with the Competition and Markets Authority on bid‑rigging risks.

turns.speaker: Lord Fuller
turns.text: Have you mapped critical raw materials, single points of failure and their mitigations?

turns.speaker: Wes Streeting
turns.text: Yes. The defence supply chain capability programme maps end-to-end supply chains and critical minerals; we are coordinating with NATO allies.

turns.speaker: Rupert Pearce
turns.text: We are building a digital twin of supply chains with real-time supplier data to spot fragility. We've taken steps like supporting Tungsten West to keep tungsten production in the UK and arranging offtake where needed.

turns.speaker: Baroness Carberry of Muswell Hill
turns.text: How will you balance 'buy British' with buying timely or superior parts from abroad?

turns.speaker: Wes Streeting
turns.text: Each procurement needs judgement on timeliness, capability, value and wider economic impact. Buying British is about jobs and growth here, but we will also work with allies to ensure collective resilience.

turns.speaker: Baroness Harding of Winscombe
turns.text: On 'always‑on' munitions factories, how will you make them commercially viable in peacetime?

turns.speaker: Rupert Pearce
turns.text: It's hard. For some items we maintain a steady baseline for training and surge later. Ukraine demand has helped keep production lines busy for several munitions; for fast‑changing items like some drones, an always‑on factory isn't practical.

turns.speaker: Baroness Valentine
turns.text: What about areas without defence growth deals and local skills shortages — how will you supply enough skilled staff?

turns.speaker: Wes Streeting
turns.text: The five existing growth deals are a start; we want to spread opportunity more widely. We will open more technical colleges and back regional plans. The defence jobs plan, coming soon, targets an extra 53,000 priority workers by 2035.

turns.speaker: Ben White
turns.text: Regional defence clusters and UK Defence Innovation teams feed local skills needs into colleges and apprenticeships; the jobs plan will set out how we close those gaps.

chapters.title: Security, testing and regulation
chapters.takeaway: The MoD is increasing classified threat briefings for industry, building testing and regulatory sandboxes, and working to define 'Britishness' and to improve test facilities for autonomy.

turns.speaker: Lord Camoys
turns.text: Western intelligence warns hostile states target defence industry and executives. Can you assure businesses of the support and protection they need?

turns.speaker: Wes Streeting
turns.text: We're treating attacks, sabotage and assassination plots as extremely serious. We provide classified briefings to security‑cleared industry leaders and work across government on protective measures.

turns.speaker: The Chair
turns.text: Regulation can be outdated and slow testing — we heard an example about lifejackets for autonomous marine vehicles. How are you addressing regulatory friction and lack of test facilities?

turns.speaker: Wes Streeting
turns.text: The Government aims to reduce unnecessary regulatory burden and the Regulatory Innovation Office has focused on defence tech. We will use sandboxes to allow safe testing without irrelevant rules.

turns.speaker: Rupert Pearce
turns.text: Test and evaluation capacity is a constraint for SMEs. We're working with regulators like the Maritime and Coastguard Agency to allow more coastal testing and to expand test facilities.

turns.speaker: Ben White
turns.text: We ran a regulatory sprint on autonomous systems; its recommendations are being implemented. The Regulating for Growth Bill will provide statutory sandboxing to ease trials in controlled areas.

turns.speaker: The Chair
turns.text: How will you define a 'British' company for procurement and 'sovereignty'?

turns.speaker: Rupert Pearce
turns.text: We are co‑designing a practical definition with industry under the DIJC, focused on where IP, jobs and growth lie, rather than a narrow legal address test.

turns.speaker: Ben White
turns.text: We've consulted many firms through trade bodies to ensure the definition has the intended consequences; the current legal test (an address in the UK) is too limited for our aims.

turns.speaker: Wes Streeting
turns.text: Politically, my concern is that taxpayer-funded defence spending translates into jobs, skills and growth felt here in Britain — that's the core of 'buy British' for me.

turns.speaker: The Chair
turns.text: Any final point you want to leave with the committee?

turns.speaker: Wes Streeting
turns.text: See the defence industrial base as an integral part of warfighting capability. We must out-innovate and out-produce adversaries. The MoD will publish more delivery plans and the new defence jobs plan; Minister Luke Pollard is a strong champion we can call on too.

turns.speaker: The Chair
turns.text: Thank you. We'll expect the reports and further engagement as we finalise our inquiry report.
